teaser: A small harbor view, painted fast, that accidentally named an entire movement.
review_notes:
Size 48 x 63 cm.
Shown April 1874 at 35 boulevard des Capucines (Nadar's former studio); Louis Leroy's review in Le Charivari coined “Impressionists”; wallpaper remark paraphrased.
Bought by Ernest Hoschedé for 800 francs in 1874, resold 1878 for 210 francs to Georges de Bellio.
Stolen from the Musée Marmottan in October 1985, recovered in Corsica in 1990.
Sun and sky of nearly equal brightness (Margaret Livingstone's observation).
Painted from a hotel window in Le Havre; a 2014 study proposed 13 November 1872, about 7:35 a.m.: stated as a proposal.

lesson.text: How long does a sunrise last? The part where the sun is a clean orange coin just above the haze, and the water has not yet turned to daylight: a few minutes, perhaps less. Claude Monet gave himself about that long to catch this one.

He was at a hotel window in Le Havre, the port in northern France where he grew up. The canvas was small, 48 by 63 centimeters (about 19 by 25 inches), small enough to cover in one sitting. Below him lay cranes, masts, steamships, and fog. He painted what he could see before it changed.

So he could not draw each ship and then color it in, the way painters were taught. There was no time. Each thing in the harbor had to be set down in a handful of strokes, and the strokes had to be right the first time.

lesson.title: How few strokes?
lesson.text: Count the brush marks as you go. Each stop is built from less paint than you would think.

spots.title: The sun
spots.text: One round dab of orange, with a slightly lighter center. It is the only hard-edged shape in the picture, and the only strongly warm color among the grays and blues.

spots.title: The reflection
spots.text: Short horizontal dashes of orange, stacked like rungs of a ladder, with gaps where the gray water shows. Each dash is one ripple catching the light.

spots.title: The rowboat
spots.text: A dark smear for the hull, two upright flicks for the people, one standing with an oar. No faces, no oarlocks. Your eye supplies them.

spots.title: The far shore
spots.text: Chimneys, masts and smoke are thin veils of blue-gray, brushed so lightly that the weave of the canvas shows through. Fog painted as fog.

lesson.text: Monet is not painting a harbor. He is painting what an eye receives from a harbor in a few minutes of dawn light.

Those ghostly shapes on the far shore are not all picturesque sailing ships. Some are factory chimneys and loading cranes. Le Havre was a busy modern port, and France was rebuilding after losing a war to Prussia in 1871. This quiet picture is also a view of industry waking up.
Researchers studied the tides, the sun's position and weather records for Le Havre and proposed an exact moment for the painting: November 13, 1872, around 7:35 in the morning.

Two years later, in April 1874, Monet and about thirty friends, tired of being refused by the official Salon, rented a photographer's former studio in Paris and held their own exhibition. He needed a title for the catalog. “View of Le Havre” did not fit a picture this vague, so he told them to put “Impression.”

A critic named Louis Leroy pounced on the word. In a mocking review he called the whole group “Impressionists,” and joked that wallpaper in its earliest stage was more finished than this seascape. The insult stuck. Within a few years the painters were using the name themselves.

The painting sold in 1874 for 800 francs. Four years later its owner went bankrupt and it was auctioned again, for just 210 francs. The buyer was a doctor, Georges de Bellio, whose family eventually gave it to the Musée Marmottan.
What Leroy saw as unfinished hides a firm structure. Monet did not have time to plan it on paper, but he chose where to stand and where to put his few dark notes.

lines.label: Three boats
lines.text: The boats step down a diagonal, each darker and sharper than the one behind. Fading objects with distance like this is called atmospheric perspective. Here the fog does the work.

lines.label: The orange drop
lines.text: Sun and reflection form one vertical, a little right of center. It anchors a picture that otherwise has no firm horizon and no solid ground.

lesson.text: The darkest, sharpest boat sits close to that orange line, near the center. Everything precise is gathered there. Everywhere else, edges melt away, just as they do at the corner of your eye.

The sun looks like the brightest thing in the picture, but it is almost exactly as light as the sky around it. In a black-and-white photograph of the painting, it nearly disappears. Only its color sets it apart, which may be why it seems to shimmer.
Monet left one more trace of his hurry at the bottom of the canvas, and it tells you he was satisfied with what he had caught.
Monet signed and dated this picture. Where?

spots.title: Claude Monet 72
spots.text: Dark brushed letters in the lower left, written straight into the wet-looking water, with “72” for 1872. Painters rarely sign a mere study. Monet considered this one done.

lesson.text: In October 1985 armed thieves walked into the Musée Marmottan in daylight and took nine paintings, this one included. It was missing for five years before police recovered it in Corsica in 1990.

Today it hangs in that same museum in Paris, a small canvas under heavy protection. The harbor of 1872 is gone: Le Havre was bombed flat in 1944. The few minutes Monet looked at it are still there, and they gave a name to the way painters would look at the world for the next half century.

quiz.question: Where did Monet paint this view?
options: In the port of Le Havre
quiz.explanation: He worked from a hotel window in Le Havre, where he grew up.

quiz.question: How did the Impressionists get their name?
options: From a critic mocking this painting's title
From the name of their art school
quiz.explanation: Louis Leroy turned the word “Impression” into a joke that stuck.

quiz.question: How is the sun's reflection painted?
options: With tiny dots of many colors
With short horizontal dashes of orange
quiz.explanation: The dashes are stacked like ladder rungs, with gray water between them.

quiz.question: What is surprising about the sun's brightness?
options: It is far lighter than anything else
It is about as light as the sky around it
It was painted with gold leaf
quiz.explanation: Only its color sets it apart; in black and white it nearly vanishes.

quiz.question: What happened to the painting in 1985?
options: It was stolen from the museum
It was damaged in a fire
It was sold at auction for 210 francs
quiz.explanation: Armed thieves took it, and it was recovered in 1990.

quiz.question: What does the diagonal of three boats show?
options: Objects fading with distance in the fog
quiz.explanation: Each boat is darker and sharper than the one behind, which is atmospheric perspective.

facts.text: Impression, Sunrise is a very large canvas, over two meters wide.
facts.explanation: It is small, about 48 by 63 centimeters.

facts.text: The painting lost value between 1874 and 1878, selling for 210 francs after first fetching 800.
facts.explanation: Its bankrupt owner's sale brought barely a quarter of the first price.

facts.text: The far shore shows only old sailing ships, with no sign of industry.
facts.explanation: Chimneys and cranes of a modern port stand in the fog.
